question: Running the spec-directed `changelog fold` emptied both changelog.d/ corpora and turned 15 tests in ai_router/tests/test_changelog_partition.py red. It also exposed a real defect in shipped code: check() returns [] immediately in its empty-corpus branch when foldedAt is stamped, so it never compares the recorded originalSha256 against the rendered document -- from the moment a release is folded until the next fragment is added, the round-trip guard verifies nothing, and an edit to released history passes silently. The spec's Non-goals forbid any product code change in this release set. Fix the tests only, fix the code too, or unfold?
decision: Test-only. Repair the 15 tests so the falsifier battery keeps its power post-fold (the sandbox fixture seeds a real-prose corpus when the live one is folded; the non-empty-corpus guard accepts the foldedAt contract check() already ships; the pending-region assertions state what a folded corpus makes unavailable rather than asserting it vacuously), and pin the check() gap with one strict-xfail falsifier so it is executably visible and turns green the day it is closed. The code defect is recorded as a residual with a named owner. ai_router runtime bytes are unchanged and 1.0.0 ships as described.

options.option: Test-only fix + recorded residual (chosen)
options.consequence: The spec's no-product-code Non-goal is respected literally and in spirit; pytest goes green; the tagged 1.0.0 artifact is byte-identical in its runtime code to what was verified before this session; the check() gap ships unfixed but is pinned by an executable falsifier and owned by a follow-on set rather than living in prose.

options.option: Also close the check() gap (~6 lines, symmetric with code already present)
options.consequence: The guard would actually guard post-fold before 1.0.0 publishes, but it waives a Non-goal written precisely to stop a release set from changing the artifact it is describing, grows the release diff, and owes a delta-scoped remediation-review after verification. The same test work is required either way -- the code fix alone repairs only 3 of the 15 failures.

options.option: Unfold and ship 17 loose fragments
options.consequence: No test or code change and the suite returns green untouched, but spec step 2's deliverable -- a tagged commit carrying real version sections rather than loose fragments -- is simply not delivered, and the Set 125 security entry lands in a fragment file instead of the release notes.

operator_attestation: Operator ruled 2026-08-15, presented with all three options and their consequences: take the test-only fix, respect the release set's no-product-code Non-goal, and carry the check() post-fold gap as a named residual rather than widening the tagged diff.
reasoning: The authority is the operator's because the consequence is external and hard to reverse: it decides what bytes go to PyPI as 1.0.0. The orchestrator's role was to establish that test changes are unavoidable under every option (11 of the 15 failures are falsifiers with no corpus left to plant into, which no code fix restores), so the real question was only whether the release absorbs a product-code fix as well. Operator ruled 2026-08-15: it does not.

question: The declared run-of-record command for pytest is `.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pytest ai_router/tests -q -n auto`, and `-n auto` is the addopts default in pytest.ini. The operator directed on 2026-08-10 that parallelism be capped at 8 and never run at auto/all-cores (20 on this machine), because an unfixed bug starves the OS. Run the declared command verbatim, or the capped one?
decision: Run `-n 8`, overriding the `-n auto` default on the command line. Every test in the declared input set still executes and is still asserted; only the worker count differs. Recorded here so the composition of the run of record is auditable rather than presented as the declared command run verbatim.

options.option: -n 8, the operator's cap (chosen)
options.consequence: Identical specs, identical assertions, identical pass/fail set; slower than 20 workers and faster than serial. Honours a standing operator directive that exists because of a real machine-level failure, and the deviation is journaled.

options.option: -n auto, the declared command verbatim
options.consequence: Matches the recorded command string exactly, but disregards a live operator directive and risks starving the OS on a 20-core machine during a ~49-minute run -- the precise failure the cap was set to avoid.

reasoning: project-guidance G-004: a workflow rule protects an outcome, and the outcome the run of record protects is 'did every test execute and pass', not 'did it happen at a particular worker count'. Parallelism is an optimization and was never part of the contract under test -- the same reasoning by which the repo already rules that falling back to serial execution is not a verification reduction. This licenses a different route to the same evidence, never less evidence. Set 117 is the set that should reconcile pytest.ini's `-n auto` default with the operator's cap so this deviation stops recurring.

question: Layer 3 failed 32/32 at Electron launch. The first read was 'the harness cannot run in this environment', which would have put the close to an operator waiver. Waive Layer 3, or find out why?
decision: Diagnose, then run it. Root cause: this orchestrator's shell is a VS Code-hosted terminal, so it carries ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 and the VSCODE_* IPC family. Those flip the launched Code.exe into Node/CLI mode -- it parses --extensionDevelopmentPath as a CLI flag and exits 9, which is Node's own bad-option exit code. Proven both ways on the same machine and build: with the vars present a bare `Code.exe --user-data-dir=<tmp> --new-window` exits 9; with VSCODE_*/ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE removed from the child environment the same command opens a window and stays alive. Layer 3 is therefore run with those variables stripped from the parent process, which is the same environment the suite has always had when run from an ordinary terminal.

options.option: Diagnose and run with a scrubbed environment (chosen)
options.consequence: Real Layer 3 evidence against the actual change set, no waiver, no verification reduction. Costs ~13 minutes plus the diagnosis. Identical command and specs; only the inherited IDE pollution is removed.

options.option: Operator-attested waiver for Layer 3
options.consequence: Closes today, but reduces verification on the exact class G-024 exists for (a package.json edit once shipped an icon shape VS Code rejected) -- and would have done so to route around an environment artifact rather than a real defect. The operator declined this and was right to: the suite has run on this machine many times.

options.option: Defer the close until a follow-on set fixes the harness
options.consequence: Slips the release for what turned out to be an inherited environment variable, not a harness defect.

reasoning: The operator pushed back on the waiver -- the suite has run on this machine many times -- and the pushback was correct. The failure said nothing about the change set OR about the harness; it was the orchestrator's own shell. Worth recording because the harness already guards against exactly this (electronEnv is a strict allowlist, and its comment names the ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE/VSCODE_* case by name), and the guard did not survive: stripping the variables from the parent shell was required to make the suite run. An orchestrator working inside VS Code -- which is how this framework is meant to be driven -- hits this every time. Recorded as a residual for the harness owner.

question: CORRECTION to the immediately preceding decision record. That entry named ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE / VSCODE_* pollution from the orchestrator's VS Code-hosted shell as the root cause of Layer 3's 32/32 launch failures. Stripping those variables did NOT fix it. What is actually wrong?
decision: A VS Code installer is STUCK on this machine and holds the machine-wide `vscode-updating` Inno Setup mutex. CodeSetup-stable-a5b500951314efd502d07465bd138dfbd714a960.exe (pid 30800) and its .tmp child (pid 34340) have been running since 04:36:24 on 2026-08-15. Every VS Code launch prints 'checkInnoSetupMutex: vscode-updating is held, waiting up to 30s for setup to finish...', waits, and dies without ever creating a window -- which is why all 32 specs failed at ~34.3s (30s wait + overhead), identically, regardless of VS Code version, worker count, shell, or environment. The operator confirmed a pending-update button in their editor. Resolution is the OPERATOR's: release the mutex (dismiss/cancel the installer, or apply the update and restart), then re-run Layer 3. No harness or product change is implicated in the failure itself.

options.option: Correct the record and name the real cause (chosen)
options.consequence: The prior entry stays on the ledger and is superseded rather than rewritten, so the wrong turn is auditable. The next orchestrator meets the true cause and a 30-second check (look for a running CodeSetup process) instead of re-deriving an environment theory.

options.option: Leave the earlier entry standing
options.consequence: The journal would assert a root cause that was tested and disproved, and the next Layer 3 failure on any machine would be misdiagnosed the same way -- the exact defect class this session spent its verification budget removing from the release notes.

reasoning: Three claims in the superseded entry were wrong and are withdrawn. (1) The ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE pollution is REAL in the orchestrator's shell and did produce 'bad option:' output in a hand-rolled Git Bash probe, but it never reached the harness: electronEnv is a strict allowlist that already excludes it, so it was never the cause of the suite failing. (2) 'A bare Code.exe exits with code 9' was an artifact of that same hand-rolled probe, not evidence about the harness. (3) The probe that reported 'window opened, process alive at 20s' proved nothing -- 20s is INSIDE the 30s mutex wait, and process liveness was checked instead of window existence. The operator caught this from the outside: they said the launches behaved as if headless because no window ever appeared on their desktop, which is exactly what a mutex-blocked launch looks like and what the timing confirms. Recorded because the standing lesson here is procedural: liveness is not readiness, and a 30-second wait swallowed the only line that named the cause.

question: The close backstop (round 5, delta-scoped remediation-review, gpt-5-6-sol, anthropic excluded) returned one Major -- 'The claimed Marketplace and changelog correction is absent from the fix delta' -- and the close gate refused. The orchestrator disputes it. Accept, dismiss, or seek a third opinion?
decision: DISMISSED as a false positive, on operator adjudication with deterministic falsifying evidence. The finding is a delta-scoping artifact: the round's baseline is the round-4 COMPLETION anchor (9e4871a6a318), which already contains the corrections, so the delta from baseline to current tree legitimately carries no hunk for package.json or ai_router/CHANGELOG.md -- it carries only the two changelog .baseline.json digest re-stamps. The verifier reasoned correctly from the bundle it was given and then inferred absent-from-delta = absent-from-code. Session 1 closes with --manual-verify carrying this adjudication; the substantive verdict of record remains round 4's VERIFIED (fix accepted, 0 findings).

options.option: Adjudicate false positive and close with attestation (chosen)
options.consequence: The release closes on evidence that is checkable by anyone: the two surfaces carry the required disclosure at HEAD. The round-5 artifact stays on the ledger unedited, and this adjudication sits beside it, so a later reader sees the finding AND why it was not actioned.

options.option: Third-provider opinion before adjudicating
options.consequence: One more routed call (~$0.15) to have an independent verifier accept the dismissal rather than the orchestrator's reasoning. Legitimate and sanctioned, but the falsifying evidence here is deterministic file content rather than a judgment call, so a third model would be adjudicating something a `git show` settles.

options.option: Treat the finding as real and edit the copy again
options.consequence: Would rewrite text that rounds 3 and 4 already reviewed and accepted, to fix a defect that is not present, and would exceed the remediation-review bound. Churn presented as diligence.

operator_attestation: Operator adjudicated 2026-08-15, shown the finding, the dismissal reason, the delta-scoping context the verifier saw, and the git-show evidence at HEAD: dismiss as a false positive and close Session 1 with --manual-verify. The round-5 artifact is preserved unedited.
reasoning: C-003 forbids rejecting a blocking finding on the orchestrator's own reasoning and allows exactly three exits: independent verifier acceptance, deterministic falsifying evidence, or operator adjudication. This dismissal rests on the second and the third together. The evidence, reproducible at any time: `git show HEAD:tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/package.json` yields a description reading 'plus routed verification before every close, normally cross-provider, recorded as evidence you can check' -- no unconditional independence claim -- and `git show HEAD:ai_router/CHANGELOG.md` contains the block headed 'It is not cross-provider in every case, and this release does not claim it is', naming the DIRECT_API configuration, the same-provider substitution, the verification_qualification stamp, and the scope limits. That is the acceptance criterion satisfied verbatim. TWO UPSTREAM DEFECTS this exposed, both recorded as residuals rather than fixed here: (1) post_round_delta classified the two .baseline.json files as 'not under any declared test surface' and therefore shipped-code, which forced the delta-scoped round at all -- but run_of_record affected lists both paths as pytest inputs (pytest covers `ai_router/` and `tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/changelog.d/`), so the two classifiers disagree about the same paths. (2) A delta-scoped remediation-review is handed a claims context describing the whole session's work and a bundle containing only the delta; nothing tells it that a claim satisfied BEFORE the baseline will be absent from the diff by construction, so 'the claim is contradicted by the presented ground truth' is a conclusion the framing invites. DECLARED AS A VERIFICATION REDUCTION, deliberately. The substantive cross-provider verification did happen and passed -- round 4, VERIFIED, fix accepted, 0 findings -- but closing with --manual-verify substitutes an operator attestation for the machine-settled evidence chain the close gate would otherwise require, and that is a reduction whatever the substance behind it. The journal refused the first attempt at this record for declaring effect=none while naming --manual-verify, and the refusal was correct.

question: The framework makes addition cheap and removal expensive. A module cannot be taken out without also taking out its tests, and taking out a test has so far been treated as falling inside the hard human-only carve-out, which an orchestrator may never self-authorize. Does a test whose only subject is code that no longer exists fall inside that carve-out, or outside it?
decision: OUTSIDE it. A test whose only subject is deleted code exercises nothing that ships, so retiring it alongside its subject leaves coverage of live code unchanged and is not the class of act the carve-out exists to stop. The carve-out continues to bind, unchanged, wherever live code loses coverage. Paired with an extension of the existing rule 'no gate is added without deleting one' from gates to MODULES: a module that arrives owes a module that leaves. Precondition, and it is the whole ruling: the subject must actually be gone. A test whose subject was moved, renamed, folded into another module, or merely stopped being called still has a live subject, and removing it is still a coverage reduction that needs the operator.

options.option: Rule it outside the carve-out, with the subject-is-gone precondition (chosen)
options.consequence: A paring set can retire a deleted module's tests in the same pass as the module, without an operator stop per file. The next such set inherits a decision instead of re-litigating one. The exposure is a mislabelled deletion -- a test recorded as orphaned whose subject is really alive somewhere else -- which the precondition addresses and a diff can settle.

options.option: Leave it inside the carve-out
options.consequence: Preserves the simplest possible rule: no test leaves without the operator. It also preserves the measured behaviour that produced this question -- the corpus only ever grows, deletion stays the expensive direction, and modules scheduled for removal survive and get larger. The operator pays an approval per file for deletions that remove no coverage of anything that runs.

options.option: Automate it: a gate that proves the subject is gone before allowing the test to go
options.consequence: Strictly better than a written rule if it works, and it is the direction this ruling should eventually take. It is also a build, with its own falsifiers and its own failure modes, and it cannot be specified before the policy it enforces exists. Deferred deliberately, not rejected.

operator_attestation: Operator ruling, recorded at their direction: Set 133 spec, Session 2 step 3, which states the ruling, names authority=human, and supplies the reasoning and the measured symptoms to record. The spec was authored and approved by the operator on 2026-08-15.
reasoning: Declared verification_effect='none' deliberately, and the declaration is the primary control here, so it is worth saying exactly what it asserts: retiring a test whose subject is deleted changes the coverage of live code by zero, because there is no live code under it. It does not assert that deleting tests is generally safe, and it does not touch the carve-out anywhere a running line loses its test. MEASURED SYMPTOMS behind the ruling: the suite stands at 4,640 tests growing at roughly +29 test functions per day, and ZERO guards have ever been retired -- the corpus has only ever grown. Set 116 S3 demoted five gates from blocking to warning and deliberately deleted none of them. Of six modules scheduled for deletion, three went and the three survivors GREW: contract_gate 1,158 -> 1,319, spec_admission 403 -> 1,082, replacement_gate 546 -> 652 lines. The three current figures were re-derived in this session (wc -l: 1319 / 1082 / 652) rather than inherited from the spec; the 4,640 count is the operator's 2026-08-15 measurement, and this session's own run of record collected 4,670 (4,664 passed / 5 skipped / 1 xfailed), so the growth claim holds and the absolute number moves. WHY THE OPERATOR AND NOT THE ORCHESTRATOR: the trade-off is between retention conservatism and the cost of a corpus that can only grow, and neither side is derivable from the code -- it is a value call about what the framework should be like to work in, which is the underivable-value-trade-off class. It is not recorded under the verification-reduction line because the ruling's content is that this class of removal is not one; recording it there would require declaring an effect the ruling denies. Both readings are on the record here so an auditor can disagree with the label and still see the whole decision. THIS IS A RULING, NOT AN IMPLEMENTATION: no code changed in this session, no test was deleted under it, and the first set to apply it should carry the subject-is-gone evidence per deletion in its own journal.

question: Every OpenAI model on this seat returns 429 Too Many Requests -- probed individually across gpt-5-6-sol, gpt-5-5, gpt-5-4 and gpt-5-6-luna, so it is an account-level limit, not one model and not a burst. The orchestrator is anthropic, so anthropic is excluded from verifying its own work, which leaves google as the only reachable different-provider verifier. Google's routable ceiling in this registry is tier 2 (gemini-2.5-pro) where the pinned verifier gpt-5-6-sol is tier 3. Run the round against google at tier 2, or stop the session?
decision: Run the round against google. This is rung 2 of the documented verifier-failure escalation ladder -- retry the pinned verifier once, then fall back to the remaining cross-provider verifier -- and it was reached only after three full attempts on the pinned verifier, two of them separated by a deliberate wait to let a burst limit clear. Executed through ai_router/local-overrides.yaml with providers.openai.enabled: false, which is the sanctioned surface for exactly this: providers.<id>.enabled is on the allow-list, the file is gitignored machine state, and it never enters the commit. The override is reverted as soon as verification has been recorded, so it describes this seat during this outage and nothing else. The cross-provider guarantee is intact end to end: an anthropic orchestrator, a google verifier, every severity, full scope, with every round and every gate still in force.

options.option: Fall back to google via the local provider override (chosen)
options.consequence: The round runs cross-provider today. The verifier is gemini-2.5-pro at tier 2 rather than gpt-5-6-sol at tier 3, so the reviewing model is less capable than the pinned one, and that is stated in the disposition rather than buried. The exposure is a weaker read of a four-file documentation change whose factual claims are all independently checkable against PyPI, the gallery API, git and the run logs.

options.option: Stop the session until OpenAI clears
options.consequence: Preserves the tier-3 verifier. Costs an indefinite wait on an external quota nobody here controls, on a session whose work is already complete, and leaves the release record uncommitted in a working tree in the meantime. The ladder exists precisely so that a provider outage does not become a stopped session.

options.option: Disable route()'s internal verification so the pinned verifier can be reached without its secondary call
options.consequence: REJECTED and not attempted. That would turn off a verification control to work around an outage, which is the hard human-only carve-out and is never self-authorizable. Named here so the record shows it was considered and refused rather than never seen.

reasoning: Declared verification_effect='none' because nothing is skipped: the session still gets a full different-provider adversarial round at every severity, which is what the no-skip mandate protects. What changes is WHICH different provider, and the ladder in docs/ai-led-session-workflow.md names that substitution as the correct response to a provider failure -- so this defers to an existing gate rather than inventing an exception, which is why tiebreak 4 is the line recorded. Stated plainly so an auditor can disagree: gemini-2.5-pro is a tier-2 model and gpt-5-6-sol is tier 3, so the reviewing model IS less capable than the pin, and someone could reasonably call that a reduction. Two things bound it. First, the evidence under review is four documentation files whose every factual claim is externally checkable -- a PyPI JSON response, a gallery API response, two git tags, four workflow run ids -- so this is close to the cheapest possible round to run with a smaller model. Second, the alternative rungs further down the same ladder are all worse: decompose the prompt, verify against a description of the work instead of the work, or log a Major and proceed unverified. DIAGNOSIS WORTH KEEPING: the round did not fail where it appeared to. verify_session selected gemini-pro correctly under the anthropic exclusion and the call still died against api.openai.com, because route() makes a SECOND call to verify its own output and that secondary call was choosing the rate-limited provider. Excluding openai from both halves is what actually unblocks it. TOOL GAP FOUND BY HITTING IT, recorded as a residual and NOT fixed here because this set forbids product code: verify_session hardcodes exclude_providers to the orchestrator's own provider (verify_session.py line 3345) and offers no flag to add a second one, so the ladder rung it prints in its own failure message -- fall back to the remaining cross-provider verifier -- has no mechanism behind it. The only way to take that rung today is a config override the failure message never mentions.

question: The preceding decision in this journal said the fallback to google would be executed through ai_router/local-overrides.yaml with providers.openai.enabled: false. It was tried and it DID NOT WORK -- the round selected gpt-5-6-sol anyway and died against api.openai.com exactly as before. What actually takes rung 2 of the ladder, and how should the earlier record be treated?
decision: SUPERSEDE the mechanism, keep the ruling. The fallback to google stands and its reasoning is unchanged; only the means was wrong, and the earlier entry stays on the ledger unedited beside this one rather than being rewritten. What works is running the one command with DABBLER_OPENAI_API_KEY absent from the process environment. The router consults key AVAILABILITY, not providers.<id>.enabled, when it builds the candidate pool: with no key it prints 'disabled provider(s) openai (no DABBLER_OPENAI_API_KEY); dispatching with anthropic, google' and selects gemini-pro for task_type=session-verification under the anthropic exclusion. Confirmed live before re-running -- a probe returned gemini-2.5-pro, tier 2, cost $0.000109. The variable is cleared for that single process only; it is never unset in the Windows User environment and nothing on disk changes. The gitignored local-overrides.yaml written for the failed attempt has been deleted.

options.option: Clear the key for the single verifying process (chosen)
options.consequence: Reaches the ladder's rung 2 through the mechanism the router actually consults, with no file changed and no persistent state touched. It is also an accurate statement rather than a fiction: this seat genuinely cannot call OpenAI right now.

options.option: Set is_enabled: false on the openai models in router-config.yaml
options.consequence: REJECTED. That file is tracked product configuration, it is not on the local-override allow-list, and a release-records session that forbids product code has no business editing the shipped model registry to get its own round to run.

options.option: Declare verification unavailable and stop to the operator now
options.consequence: Correct if no cross-provider verifier could be reached at all. One demonstrably can, so stopping would spend the operator's attention on an outage the documented ladder already answers.

reasoning: Recorded as its own entry, superseded-not-rewritten, because the previous record asserted a mechanism that turned out to be false and this journal is an audit trail rather than a summary -- the same treatment Session 1 gave its own wrong diagnosis of the Layer 3 failure. SECOND TOOL GAP, and it is the more serious of the two found here, recorded as a residual and NOT fixed because this set forbids product code: providers.<id>.enabled is explicitly on the local-override allow-list in config.py, and setting it to false changed nothing about which model was selected. An operator reading that allow-list would reasonably believe they had turned a provider off. It loads, it validates, it is reported as applied, and the pinned verifier is chosen from that provider regardless -- a control that appears to work and does not. Paired with the first gap (verify_session hardcodes exclude_providers to the orchestrator's own provider and offers no flag to add another), the ladder rung that verify_session PRINTS in its own failure message is reachable today only by clearing an environment variable that the message never mentions. Owner: a follow-on router set; natural companion to the step-3.5 model-id fix already owed.
